## Key Features {.unnumbered}

- **What is unique:** a large, fully simulated, multi-file dataset for linking individual people, with cross-file ground truth (every record carries a `simulant_id`, so missed-match and false-match rates of any method can be computed exactly rather than estimated), designed to capture the record matching challenges faced by a Florida-scale cancer data system.

- **Why created:** linkage software for cancer registries must be developed and tested on names, dates of birth, addresses and SSNs, which are exactly the identifiers that confidentiality rules prevent registries from releasing.

- **Details:** a simulated Florida drawn from the 50\,518\,675 simulated people recorded as residents in the simulated 2020, 2030 or 2040 censuses, including a simulated registry of 5\,000\,000 records whose age and sex distribution is that of the cases reported by the Florida Cancer Data System, and researcher finder files of 500\,000 and 100\,000 records drawn from residents in 2040.

- **Data linkage:** the larger finder file includes 100\,000 people who are also in the registry and the smaller finder file includes 20\,000. There is no overlap between the finder files.

- **Main categories of data:** simulated person-level identifiers including name, date of birth, sex, street-address fields, SSN, race/ethnicity, and a diagnosis date on each registry record, carrying realistic synthetic noise (typos, nicknames, month/day swaps, blanks, duplications).

- **Access:** direct download under a permissive licence with a DOI.

# Methods {#sec-methods}

This section describes how we extracted a simulated Florida population (@sec-source), how we generated three files from that extract (@sec-design), how we noised each file and formatted them for release (@sec-noise), how we validated our work (@sec-qa), and the measures that we report (@sec-characterise). The mechanics that only a rebuilder needs are in @sec-build-details.

## Source population and the Florida extract {#sec-source}

The records come from pseudopeople, a Python package for generating simulated versions of the data sets that record linkage runs on [@pseudopeople_software; @haddock2024simulated]. Behind it is a microsimulation of the United States, initialised to the size and demographics of the country in 2020 and run forward through 2040 with births, deaths and moves, in which each simulated person, a "simulant" in pseudopeople's vocabulary, carries a `simulant_id` and is observed by simulated data-collecting systems: a decennial census in 2020, 2030 and 2040, the Social Security Administration, tax filings and others [@haddock2024simulated]. pseudopeople ships with a small sample population, which is all this document executes; the full population is available on request [@keyes2026governance].



pseudopeople can generate one state and year of the census directly, but it has no interface for the sampling design we needed, quotas by age and sex and controlled overlaps between files, and its Social Security observer has no state filter, so we did the selection ourselves. We used DuckDB 1\.5\.4 to read the census observer's Parquet files directly, kept the Florida rows of the three censuses, one per person per census, and built two pools from them. We created a "last-seen pool" that holds every person ever recorded in Florida, taken once at their latest census, and is the frame for the simulated registry; it is more than twice the size of Florida's population at any one census, because it keeps everyone who died or left the state between censuses, which is what a registry does with the cases it has registered. We used only the residents from 2040 as the frame for the finder files, since a researcher's cohort is often a roster of living people at one time. We joined SSNs from the Social Security observer on the identifier, and we then ran pseudopeople on only the rows we selected, to make our Florida-scale computation faster than a national-scale pseudopeople run. Addresses in the source are real Florida city names and ZIP codes with simulated streets, so the released addresses place people in real cities at no real location [@haddock2024simulated], and the simulation knows nothing about cancer. The registry is a sample of people chosen to have a registry's age and sex pattern, not a model of disease.

## Cohort design and sampling {#sec-design}

From these source populations, we sampled a simulated registry of 5\,000\,000 people with the age and sex distribution of the cases FCDS reported between 1995 and 2023 [@pseudopeople_issue205], and finder files of 500\,000 and 100\,000 people, of whom 100\,000 and 20\,000 also appear in the registry, with no person in both finder files. The age and sex target is the count column of an FCDS table of reported cases by sex and 18 age groups, taken as shares<!-- provenance: supplied by the second author; confirm report, diagnosis years and denominator at source before publication (OUTLINE decision #7) -->, and each of the 36 strata contributes an exact quota, which we filled using a reproducible random draw within each stratum. We preferred the registry's own case shares to a general population target because they are the age and sex pattern a real linkage against FCDS will meet.

Since we sampled our finder files from the simulated 2040 census, overlapping entries in the registry are only possible for registry members sampled from the 2040 census as well. pseudopeople's default row noise removes an unpredictable number of rows, so for every cohort we sampled an oversized population, then added additional noise, and then trimmed back to the exact target size using a reproducible random sample that also keeps the finder files disjoint. This produced the ground truth for scoring: a registry row and a finder row that carry the same identifier form a "true pair", a match a linkage should find, and every other pairing of a registry row with a finder row is a true non-match; people last seen in 2020 or 2030 appear in the registry alone, and are all non-matches a linkage must reject. Each true pair represents one simulant recorded twice, with different noise for the registry and the finder files, so its two records differ only by injected noise, with no move, ageing or change of surname between them, which is the easiest case a linkage can face (@sec-discussion).

## Noise, schema and packaging {#sec-noise}

We used pseudopeople's default noise suite, in which each column carries several mechanisms at 1% of cells apiece (a first name can be left blank, replaced by a nickname or a fake name, or altered by a phonetic, optical-character-recognition or typing error; a date of birth can have its month and day swapped, digits miswritten or be copied from a household member; a categorical field can take a wrong category) and rows go missing by non-response at 1\.45%, and we made two additions. We raised the blanking of the six address fields to 5% in the finder files and left it at 1% in the registry, and we noised the SSN ourselves, because pseudopeople does not noise that column in the census: we blanked SSNs to a target share of 20% in the finder files and 5% in the registry, counting the people who never held a number in the simulation before blanking anyone else, and we swapped one adjacent pair of digits in 1% of the finder files' remaining SSNs, a mechanism pseudopeople lacks (@sec-build-details). We took these rates from the second author's specification of what a researcher's finder file looks like against the registry's consolidated file, which is usually the cleaner of the two [@qiao2023lexisnexis], and we do not defend them as realistic beyond that. What we left out is as important as what we put in: we gave the SSN no wrong digits and no relative's number, we changed no surnames, we applied the noise symmetrically between the files and independently across fields where a real cohort has habits of its own, and we wrote both files in one format; we weigh these choices in @sec-discussion. We switched off pseudopeople's row duplication, which gives a child a second row at a guardian's address, so every file has exactly one row per person, and these files do not exercise within-file duplicate detection.

We released in every row the identifier and the fields linkage relies on: first name, middle initial, last name, date of birth, sex, race/ethnicity, street number, street name, unit number, city, state, ZIP code and SSN, keeping race/ethnicity because FCDS's own submission layout carries it [@fcds_linkage_layout]. We covered every field in either of FCDS's minimum matching sets, but not the layout's maiden name, alias or birthplace. We gave each registry row a diagnosis date, a day drawn uniformly within the year of the record's census, so that age at diagnosis is within a year of the age the quota was matched on, at the cost that diagnoses heap on three years (@sec-discussion); a finder file is a cohort roster, so we gave it no such date. We wrote the files as CSV with a header row and blanks as empty fields, placed a data dictionary inside the zip with every field's format, blank convention and noise mechanisms, built the zip so that its bytes depend only on its contents, and added to the deposit a manifest of MD5 and SHA-256 digests and the configuration file with every seed and target (@sec-build-details). This profile describes dataset version 0\.4, which we built with pseudopeople 1\.2\.8.

## Quality assurance {#sec-qa}

We developed four checks to run on this data, and we report their outcomes in @sec-structure and @sec-population. Reproducibility: the build is a pure function of the configuration's seeds, so we built the release twice, on different nodes, and compared the digests of every file. Scale: we compared the 2020 extract with Florida's official 2020 census count<!-- needs a Census Bureau citekey -->, the one external check available to a simulated population. Composition: we computed the age and sex composition of each file from the source's true ages rather than the noised dates of birth, compared the registry's with the FCDS shares we drew it to, recording the largest deviation of any stratum, and compared the finder files' with that of the 2040 Florida pool; agreement with FCDS checks that the sampler did what we told it, not that the data are faithful. Face validity: we tabulated the three most common first names in each age and sex group and read a sample of true pairs side by side, which is where the noise mechanisms show themselves one record at a time.

## Characterising the data {#sec-characterise}

We report five kinds of measure in @sec-results, all of which we computed on the released files with scripts archived alongside the pipeline. Error structure: for each field, we measured the share of values blank in each file against the rate we set for it and, among true pairs, the share whose two values are present and identical character for character and the share with a blank on either side; we counted the finder-file SSNs with two adjacent digits swapped; we ran sentinel checks for dates of birth that do not parse as calendar dates, Doe-pattern names, repeated-digit SSNs and SSNs outside the ranges the SSA issues; and we tabulated SSN blankness by race/ethnicity and by age at diagnosis. Quasi-identifier uniqueness: we measured the share of registry people whose first name, last name and date of birth, last name and date of birth, or ZIP code, date of birth and sex is shared by no one else in the file, and the share who share a full name with someone. A deterministic baseline: we scored 11 exact-agreement rules, each a set of fields, or two sets joined by "or", on which both records must agree after lower-casing and trimming, against the identifier as precision and recall, which we also report as false-match and missed-match rates [@lam2024synthetic]; we do not rank rules by F1 [@hand2018fmeasure] and we omit specificity, which is uninformative when true non-matches grow with the product of the file sizes [@christen2007quality]. We included the two field sets FCDS's Procedure Guide requires a submission to carry [@fdoh_fcds_procedure_guide_2007] and the two in its current Data Linkage Record Layout [@fcds_linkage_layout], as exact rules and not as FCDS's own procedure, and we treat exact agreement as a floor rather than a straw man, since deterministic algorithms run in production linkages [@enewold2020seermedicare; @doidge2018demystifying]. Stratified baselines: we recomputed three of the rules within race/ethnicity groups of the finder record; we injected the noise without regard to race, so any differential is inherited from the source population, chiefly through who holds an SSN. Blocking feasibility: we counted the candidate pairs and the share of true pairs retained when comparisons are restricted to records that agree on the full date of birth, or on the first letter of the last name with the year of birth, the first numbers a probabilistic user needs for planning compute.

# Results {#sec-results}

We describe the released files first (@sec-structure), then the people in them (@sec-population), the errors in their fields (@sec-errors) and how hard those errors make the files to link with exact rules (@sec-difficulty).

## Structure, contents, and where the data are held {#sec-structure}

This data resource is a zip archive containing three comma-separated data files and a data dictionary, to be deposited on Zenodo under a DOI that will be minted before publication<!-- OUTLINE run-list item 10 -->. The high-level characteristics of the files are described in @tbl-release: a simulated registry of 5\,000\,000 people and two finder files of 500\,000 and 100\,000 people. All three are drawn from Florida residents in the simulated 2020, 2030 or 2040 census, a pool of 50\,518\,675 distinct simulated people.  The larger finder file shares 100\,000 people with the registry, 20% of its records, and the smaller shares 20\,000, the same 20% share; the two finder files share no people with each other, matching the overlap design described above.

The data dictionary inside the archive gives each field's type, format, blank convention, source and the noise mechanisms that touch it. The deposit also carries a manifest of MD5 and SHA-256 digests (@tbl-release gives the MD5) and the configuration file that names every seed and design target, and the pipeline that built them is archived under its own DOI<!-- OUTLINE run-list item 10: code DOI -->. A second build from the same configuration and the same source population, which is available on request (@sec-access), reproduced all three files byte for byte.

## Population characteristics {#sec-population}



The simulated registry closely matches the age and sex distribution of the cases reported to FCDS between 1995 and 2023 [@pseudopeople_issue205]. The agreement is within 0.041 percentage points in each of the 36 age and sex strata. 62% of registry records are people aged 65 or older at diagnosis and 4% are under 40; 48% are women. The finder files have the age structure of the simulated population's Florida residents in 2040 instead: 26% of the larger file are 65 or older, 43% are under 40, and 51% are female.

By race and ethnicity, people in the registry are 64% White, 17% Latino, 12% Black, 5% Asian and 3% other or multiracial (American Indian and Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander, multiracial, and unknown), compared with 55%, 21%, 12%, 7% and 4% in the larger finder file. The two finder files differ from each other by at most 0\.3 percentage points on every share reported in this section.

The three most common first names in each age group, printed at the ends of the bars in @fig-registry-age-sex, run from Liam\, Noah\, Oliver among boys under five to James\, Robert\, John among men of 85 and over, and from Olivia\, Charlotte\, Emma to Mary\, Barbara\, Patricia among girls and women.

## Error structure {#sec-errors}



@tbl-errors gives the error structure field by field: the share of values that are blank in the registry and in the larger finder file, against the blanking rate set for each, and, among the 100\,000 true pairs, the share of pairs whose two records agree exactly when both have a value and the share with a blank on either side. Agreeing exactly means the two values are the same string, character for character. The error structure of the smaller finder file matches that of the larger on every figure in the table to within 0\.8 percentage points.

SSNs are blank in 20\.0% of finder records, the rate FCDS specified, and in 5\.68% of registry records against a specified 5%. The build blanked no registry SSN, so every blank there is a person who never held one in the source population, where coverage varies with age: 3\.8% of registry records for people under 40 at diagnosis lack an SSN against 6\.4% for people of 40 to 64, and the registry's ages are the ones with the least coverage, which is why its share sits above both the specification and the whole pool's 4\.18%. Blank SSNs vary by race/ethnicity: in the larger finder file 28\.9% of Asian and 23\.5% of Latino people's records have none against 17\.8% of White people's, and in the registry the shares are 21\.5%, 15\.2% and 1\.9%. Of the SSNs present in the larger finder file, 4\,001 (1\.0%) carry two adjacent digits swapped, and where a true pair has an SSN on both sides the two agree in 99\.1% of pairs.

Names and dates of birth disagree more often than SSNs do. Among true pairs with both values present, first names agree in 93\.9% of pairs, last names in 96\.0% and dates of birth in 93\.4%, and each of these fields is blank on one side in about 2\.0% of pairs. Taken together, 79\.2% of true pairs agree exactly on first name, last name and date of birth, and 77\.9% have an SSN on both sides that agrees. Address fields agree in 97\.1% of pairs with both present and are blank on one side in 5\.9%; the unit number is blank for 94% of registry records, because most addresses have none, and street numbers are blank above their set rates because some source addresses carry none.

Dates of birth are blank in 1\.0% of registry records and 1\.4% of those present do not parse as a calendar date (such as a month above twelve); 13 registry records carry a Doe-pattern name (John or Jane Doe); no SSN in any file is a single repeated digit; and 52 SSNs in the larger finder file, and none in the registry, fall in ranges the Social Security Administration does not issue.

## Linkage difficulty {#sec-difficulty}



Among the 5\,000\,000 people in the registry, 97\.0% have a first name, last name and date of birth that no one else in the file shares, 88\.8% have a unique last name and date of birth, and 81\.6% a unique ZIP code, date of birth and sex, while 47% share their full name with at least one other person.

@tbl-ladder scores exact-agreement rules on the larger finder file against the key. Agreement on first name, last name and date of birth links 79\.2% of true pairs at a precision of 99\.81%, and the SSN alone links 77\.9% at 99\.97%. The two field sets FCDS's Procedure Guide requires a submission to carry [@fdoh_fcds_procedure_guide_2007] behave differently as exact rules: name, SSN and sex makes no false matches and finds 64\.7% of true pairs, name with month and year of birth and sex admits 4\,421 false matches, 5\.5% of the pairs it proposes, and either set finds 81\.5%; the two sets of FCDS's current Data Linkage Record Layout [@fcds_linkage_layout], which both require the full date of birth, find 71\.7% together with no false matches. Name and date of birth or SSN, the best simple rule, reaches a recall of 95\.4% at a precision of 99\.82%, and last name with date of birth alone falls to a precision of 71\.0%.

Without blocking the two files present 2\.5 trillion record pairs. Blocking on the full date of birth leaves 58 million candidate pairs and keeps 91\.6% of true pairs, the pairs whose dates of birth are present and agree on both sides (@tbl-errors); blocking on the first letter of the last name with the year of birth leaves 1\.23 billion and keeps 90\.7%.

@fig-stratified splits three rules by the race/ethnicity recorded on the finder record. For first name, last name and date of birth the missed-match rate is alike across groups, from 20\.1% to 20\.9%, and the false-match rate stays below 0\.31% in every group. The SSN rule differs by group: it misses 34% of true pairs for Asian people and 29% for Latino people against 19% for White people, and the difference carries into the best simple rule, which misses 7\.0% of Asian true pairs against 4\.0% of White ones.

# Appendix: technical details of the build {#sec-build-details .appendix}

This appendix records the mechanics behind @sec-methods for anyone who wants to rebuild the files or a different cut of them; nothing here changes the picture given there. We archived the pipeline with the deposit, and every parameter named below lives in its configuration file.

**Extraction and staging.** We read the census observer's Parquet files directly with DuckDB and kept the Florida rows of the 2020, 2030 and 2040 censuses, one per person per census. We took each person's latest of those rows as the last-seen pool and the rows of 2040 as the finder pool. We wrote the rows selected for a cohort to Parquet ordered by `simulant_id` before pseudopeople saw them, because pseudopeople walks rows in file order and an unpinned order silently moves the same amount of noise onto different people, and we ordered the Social Security join the same way for the same reason. We then ran pseudopeople once per file over the staged rows, which is why a Florida-scale build completes in minutes on eight cores.

**Reproducible draws.** We made every sampling decision a pure function of the record key. A candidate's rank in a draw is the value of `md5_number_lower(simulant_id || ':' || salt || ':' || seed)`, with the seed 42 and a salt naming the draw, so within each age and sex stratum we took for the registry the quota members with the smallest hash, and for each finder file we took its overlap members from the registry's 2040 members and its filler from that year's residents outside the registry, by two further salts. We avoided the database's own random number generator because its results depend on the thread count. We set the quotas from the FCDS case shares by largest-remainder rounding, capped at the stratum's size in the pool.

**Oversampling and the stratified trim.** pseudopeople's non-response removes rows, so we drew every cohort at 1.15 times its target and trimmed it after noising with a seeded generator (seed 999) over identifier lists sorted for the same order-dependence reason. The trim takes exactly the target number of overlap members for each finder file, draws filler only from survivors outside the entire overlap pool, and keeps in the registry only the members chosen; an earlier build of ours trimmed without this stratification, kept every surviving overlap candidate and overshot its overlap targets, which is the failure the rule exists to prevent.

**SSN noise.** We joined clean SSNs from the Social Security observer; some people never held one in the simulation, and we counted those blanks first. We reached the file's target share (20% for the finder files, 5% for the registry) by blanking only the shortfall, so we left alone a file whose structural share already exceeded its target, which is one mechanism with two outcomes. In the finder files we then swapped one randomly chosen adjacent pair of digits, dashes preserved, in 1% of the SSNs still present, which can produce a number outside the ranges the Social Security Administration issues. Both steps use one numpy generator per file, seeded with the file's pseudopeople seed.

**Row duplication and what switching it off does.** pseudopeople's duplicate-with-guardian mechanism copies a child's or student's record to a guardian's address, giving one person two rows; we set it to zero. Switching any pseudopeople mechanism off re-draws the cell noise across the whole file, because pseudopeople chooses the cells to noise by a binomial draw over the number of eligible rows, so this release is a fresh realisation of the same design rather than the previous one minus a few rows.

**Diagnosis date.** We placed each registry record's diagnosis on a day drawn uniformly within its census year by a keyed hash of the identifier with seed 2026, written as `MM/DD/YYYY` like the date of birth.

**File formats and packaging.** We wrote the files as UTF-8 CSV with a header row; blanks are empty fields, never a sentinel; dates are `MM/DD/YYYY` and SSNs `ddd-dd-dddd`; we quoted a field only when it contains a comma, which is rare enough that DuckDB's CSV sniffer infers no quote character and fails unless it is named; addresses and cities are lower case, and `unincorporated` stands for unincorporated areas. We wrote the zip with fixed member timestamps and permissions, so its bytes depend only on its contents and its internal path, which carries the version, and we gave the data dictionary inside it one row per field with type, format, example, blank convention, source and the noise mechanisms that touch it. The manifest lists rows, people and MD5 and SHA-256 digests for every file and the zip.

**Definitions of the measures.** We call a date of birth unparseable when a strict `MM/DD/YYYY` parse fails, a name Doe-pattern when the first name is John or Jane and the last name Doe, and an SSN outside the issued ranges when its area is 000, 666 or 900 and above, its group 00 or its serial 0000. We compare values in the exact-agreement rules after lower-casing and trimming and evaluate each rule as a hash join between the registry and a finder file with disjunctions as unions, so the ladder runs in seconds without enumerating the pairs; we score precision and recall against the identifier, with missed-match one minus recall and false-match one minus precision. We group the finder record's race/ethnicity for the stratified baselines as White, Latino, Black, Asian, and other or unknown, the last pooling American Indian and Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander, multiracial or other, and blank. We count blocking candidates as the pairs produced by joining the files on the key, and completeness as the share of true pairs that share the key.
